title: Merging conflicting proposals risks producing an Atlas text that no voter actually approved
content:
NR-18 states the legitimacy problem with the merge power directly: "If the Core Facilitator merge parts of two approved, but conflicting AEPs, and the final merged product significantly deviates from the original intents of both, the representation of SKY voters' will becomes a compelling question."

That is the unresolved core of A.1.15.1.1, the bootstrapping provision letting the Facilitator combine "the best updates from each of the conflicting proposals." Voters ratified two specific texts under A.1.12.2.6, which requires a poll to link "a specific version of a single Atlas Edit Proposal." A synthesized third text was on no ballot. Every safeguard built around textual identity — the Frozen Period, re-triggering after edits, version-pinned poll links — is bypassed at the final step by a merge nobody voted on.

NR-18 also questions the standard by which a merger would pick winners: "If one AEP drew more support than the other, does this automatically mean the former is the best update? What if the former AEP was authored by an unknown author, while the second AEP was authored by a well-known community member with high reputation?" Vote-weight and author reputation are the two heuristics a Facilitator would naturally reach for, and the track flags both as unjustified — the second especially, since deferring to reputation converts a procedural role into a patronage one.

Finally it identifies second-order costs if merging becomes routine: "a risk of governance paralysis, where no significant progress can be made because of a loop of constant revisions and counter-revisions," and "community fatigue... due to the perception that decisions are never final," alongside the operational burden of "continuously evaluating, merging, and discarding parts of conflicting AEPs."

The underlying insight is that finality is a resource. A governance process that can always re-open an outcome spends participant attention indefinitely and never converts votes into settled rules — which is why the standing Reconciliation Process resolves incompatibility with one additional binary poll rather than with editorial synthesis.
description: NR-18 names three costs of routine merging: misrepresentation of voter will, governance paralysis through endless revision loops, and community fatigue from decisions never feeling final.
